taxonomic_note: Modern accepted placement is Bouteloua dactyloides; many Texas sources still use the long-familiar synonym Buchloe dactyloides.
look_here_first: Begin at GROUND LEVEL: buffalograss is a low stoloniferous turf forming runners that can root at nodes. Male and female flowering structures usually look very different: male plants produce short spike/raceme units on raised stems, while female plants produce compact burr-like clusters closer to the leaves. Never identify from a male head alone.
project_tracker_diagnostic: perennial mat-forming shortgrass with stolons rooting at nodes; usually dioecious with strongly different male and female inflorescences; female inflorescences compact/bur-like and often partly concealed among leaves; male inflorescences with two or three short flag-like spikes; short ciliate-membranous ligule; low dense turf/sod habit rather than a typical tall bunchgrass

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve, N. Hays County explicitly records Buchloe dactyloides (accepted Bouteloua dactyloides). Travis — Fowler (2002) documents Buchloe dactyloides as abundant in flat plots at Shield Ranch in western Travis County. Williamson — UT Austin Plant Resources Center Vascular Plants of Williamson County includes the taxon under Buchloe dactyloides; BONAP county mapping independently supports the Texas county distribution.

crew_field_steps: Check the soil-level habit: buffalograss often makes short connected sod rather than an upright tuft.
Find an aboveground horizontal stolon and photograph it rooted at a node; current habit photo does not isolate a root.
Identify flower SEX before interpreting heads. Male: small terminal units; Female: compact burs low in foliage. Photograph both separately.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Low connected turf with actual creeping stolon traced from crown to node.
True horizontal rooting stolon node at scale.
MALE raised seedhead with short flowering units (label male only after verifying actual flowers).
FEMALE compact low burr-like seedheads with scale.
Sideoats/blue grama matched head shapes to teach crew contrast.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Blue grama has a prominent curved terminal rooster-comb inflorescence and generally forms a tuft or short rhizomatous crown, while buffalograss spreads by stolons and has distinct male and female heads. Curlymesquite also mats but often has visibly hairy stolon nodes and a different flower head. Bermudagrass often has several finger-like racemes and an introduced lawn-grass context; stolons alone are not proof of buffalograss.
